title: The Three Unfortunate Lovers

full_text:
In the city of Basra lived three noble young companions: a poet, a physician, and a merchant. All three fell deeply in love with the fair Salma, the daughter of a venerable judge. Each suitor was endowed with virtue, intellect, and honor, and the maiden respected all three, unable to choose among them without breaking the hearts of the others.

One afternoon, Salma was stricken with an unprecedented and mysterious fever that baffled all the doctors of Basra. Her breath grew faint, and her father wept in despair.

The three young men met at the city gates, casting aside all rivalry to save the maiden they adored.

The merchant opened his vault and purchased a rare dried medicinal flower brought from the Himalayas at the cost of his entire inheritance. The physician applied his deepest scientific skill, distilling the flower into an exquisite life-saving elixir. The poet rode day and night across dangerous mountains to fetch fresh snow from the peaks to cool her burning brow.

Working together with selfless devotion, the three youths administered the medicine. The fever broke, Salma opened her radiant eyes, and color returned to her cheeks!

When her father, overjoyed, asked: 'Which of you shall claim her hand, for each of you has saved her life?' the three companions looked at each other with noble selflessness.

The poet said: 'The merchant gave all his wealth.' The merchant said: 'The physician gave his science.' The physician said: 'The poet gave his breath.'

Salma spoke softly from her divan: 'He who loves truly does not demand a reward for mercy. Let us remain four lifelong friends bound by a covenant of honor and mutual support.' The three suitors agreed with joyous reverence, having learned that true love is proven by selfless sacrifice rather than jealous possession.
moral: Noble love seeks the well-being and freedom of the beloved, refusing to turn affection into an instrument of possession.
